title: Almost 3-colorable graphs versus graphs with no large independent set
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: For every fixed pair of constants \(0<\eta <1\) and \(0<\varepsilon <(1- \eta )/3\), is it NP-hard to distinguish graphs G on N vertices in which an induced subgraph on at least \((1- \eta )N\) vertices is properly 3-colorable from graphs G with independence number \(\alpha (G)<\varepsilon N\)? This is the nonoverlapping promise range of the source’s Conjecture 23, whose intended demand is hardness for arbitrarily small positive \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\).
context:
Deleting at most an \(\eta\) fraction of vertices must leave a properly 3-colorable graph. The input need not be exactly 3-colorable.

Every independent set must occupy less than an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the entire graph. Merely proving that no almost-spanning subgraph can be colored with a fixed number of colors does not give this guarantee.

For every fixed k, the paper obtains a positive \(\delta\) such that it is hard, under randomized reductions, to distinguish almost 3-colorability from failure to k-color all but a \(\delta\) fraction of vertices. Conjecture 23 asks for the substantially stronger independent-set soundness condition.

The complement of an independent set is a vertex cover. The requested gap would imply hardness of approximating minimum Vertex Cover within \(3/2- \zeta\) for every fixed \(\zeta >0\), as the source explains. This consequence is motivation, not an additional target.
why: Would strengthen almost-coloring hardness enough to improve a central Vertex Cover approximation barrier, linking graph coloring promises with independent-set soundness.
status_note: The full conjecture, its definition of induced coloring and the weaker proved theorem were checked. Subsequent-result searches through 12 September 2026, including the publisher abstract of the related MFCS 2025 matrix-completion paper, did not locate this stronger independent-set gap. That later abstract is not evidence of a resolution.

progress.text: Theorem 1 establishes the almost-coloring gap under randomized reductions; Conjecture 23 asks for no independent set of any prescribed small positive fractional size.

references.title: NP-Hardness of Almost Coloring Almost 3-Colorable Graphs
references.authors: Hecht, Yahli; Minzer, Dor; Safra, Muli

definitions: G is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph, represented by its adjacency matrix or edge list. An independent set is a set of vertices containing no edge; \(\alpha (G)\) is its maximum size. The subgraph induced by \(U\subseteq V(G)\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in U. It is properly 3-colorable if a map \(U\to \{1,2,3\}\) gives adjacent vertices different labels. Define iCol\(_{3}(G)=N^{- 1}\max\){|\(U|:G[U]\) is 3-colorable}. The yes case is iCol\(_{3}(G)\ge 1- \eta\), and the no case is \(\alpha (G)/N<\varepsilon\). Fractions refer to vertices, not edges or color classes of a fixed coloring. The parameters \(\varepsilon ,\eta\) are fixed before the reduction and are not part of the graph input. In the usual deterministic NP-hardness formulation, for each pair there must be a deterministic polynomial-time map from Boolean satisfiability instances to graphs that sends satisfiable inputs into the yes case and unsatisfiable inputs into the no case. The polynomial may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\). An algorithm for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on graphs in neither case. Since a 3-colorable set has an independent subset of at least one third its size, the displayed parameter restriction ensures disjoint cases. The paper’s already proved weaker theorem allows randomized reductions; that distinction must be retained when assessing a claimed resolution.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated gap NP-hardness for every fixed admissible \(\varepsilon ,\eta\), with a reduction and its completeness and soundness guarantees, or refute the universal hardness assertion. If a claimed hardness result uses randomized reductions, state that convention explicitly and distinguish it from deterministic NP-hardness. A polynomial-time algorithm would contradict the deterministic hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); without a complexity separation, it alone is not a logical refutation of NP-hardness.
